stories.title: Bright Side Roundtable: Biggest reasons for optimism and concern in 2026-27
stories.summary: Bright Side's writers weigh in on the roster's potential, from bench depth and coaching to shooting, injuries and playmaking.
stories.detailText: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 07: Devin Booker #15 of the Phoenix Suns dribbles the ball against the Chicago Bulls during the preseason game at the United Center on October 07, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Daniel Bartel/Getty Images) | Getty Images The season begins for the Phoenix Suns this upcoming Wednesday as they make the trip to the Pacific Northwest to take on the Portland Trail Blazers. It’s a season that carries plenty of promise and uncertainty as the team looks to build upon the foundation established last year, when it won 45 games and shattered its preseason over/under of 30.5 wins. But that team ultimately finished as the eighth seed, lost its inaugural Play-In game, and was eventually swept out of the playoffs. So what does this season have in store? Over the next four days, the Bright Side of the Sun writing staff will share our thoughts on this team as we work toward making our final predictions for the upcoming season. And the first question on the board is a relatively straightforward one. What is your biggest reason for optimism heading into the season, and what is your biggest concern about this team? There’s plenty to be optimistic about when you look at this version of the Phoenix Suns. They’ve firmly established an identity and possess continuity, two things that teams around the league are constantly trying to identify and develop. That alone puts Phoenix in a position to be competitive and potentially become a difficult opponent early in the season. But my biggest reason for optimism is the intriguing balance this roster possesses between young players who will have an opportunity to develop before our very eyes and veterans who can keep the team competitive night in and night out. I’m optimistic that this blend will provide quality basketball that’s enjoyable to watch and translate into wins. As for my biggest concern, I ultimately land on the three-point shooting conundrum. This is a team that attempted the fifth most three-pointers in the NBA last season while finishing 12th in three-point shooting percentage. If that volume remains relatively consistent while the percentage declines, which I believe is a legitimate possibility given the roster construction, it’s going to create some significant challenges offensively. The Suns might find themselves needing to win more games on the defensive side of the ball than the offensive side simply because consistent perimeter shooting could be difficult to come by. Sure, there are players coming off the bench who can knock down shots from deep, but how much volume are they realistically going to receive? If the defense isn’t consistently holding opposing teams to manageable point totals, how difficult is it going to be for Phoenix to overcome deficits when the shots aren’t falling? Without reliable three-point shooting, the margin for error becomes increasingly narrow, especially when you’re trying to work your way back into games. And that concerns me. So what does the rest of the Bright Side writing staff have to say? Here are their biggest reasons for optimism and concern heading into the 2026–27 Phoenix Suns season. Brandon Duenas: The bench is the popular answer for optimism, and it’s the correct answer. We’re talking about how deep this team is despite losing its starting center until at least February. Just let that sink in. The trio of Gillespie, Kennard, and Goodwin off the bench is such a luxury. The biggest concern has to be the health issues, which contradict our strength, but also make a case for it (depth) being so necessary at the same time. Injuries happen. They’ll be better prepared for them this season. We’re just hoping they don’t snowball like they did last season. Holden Sherman: For the first time since maybe the 2021-22 season, not only do the Suns appear to have continuity and good vibes around them, but also empirical evidence that they should feel optimistic. The team shocked many last year and has reason to believe they can build on last season by keeping the roster mostly the same and upgrading at starting power forward with Miles Bridges. Bruce Veliz: The biggest reason for optimism for me is that this bench unit looks deep and can work well together. We already saw last year that Collin Gillespie can lead the unit, and players like Jordan Goodwin and Oso Ighodaro can work well off him. Not to mention the youth with Ryan Dunn, Rasheer Fleming, and Koa Peat at the forward position, it has the potential to be one of the league’s best. My biggest concern for this team is that there is still no true point guard next to Booker to help alleviate the playmaking duties. With Jalen Green working with Steve Nash this offseason, there is some light at the end of that tunnel. It’s just all about waiting to see it work in real time. Tom Mildenberger: The biggest reason for optimism is the bench. They are going to push our regular-season win total, and the Suns are going to need them to if they want to stay out of the Play-In tournament. The starting lineup is going to have games where they hit threes, and we’re all going to think, “Wow, we are really good.” But they’ll have just as many games where they don’t. You can also pencil in some inconsistency, especially early in the season, from the second-timeline guys who are going to be counted on this season, mainly Khaman, Dunn, and Rasheer. Gillespie, Kennard, Goodwin, and Oso aren’t just going to have to be good; they’ll need to be consistently good. I think they will meet that challenge in the regular season. My biggest concern will continue to be injuries. We’re already down our starting center, and Miles Bridges has already limped off the court. While he’ll be available when the games count, his preseason reps have been limited. Obviously, losing Devin Booker for an extended period would have us hitting the under, but I’m also concerned about nagging injuries. The core four need to gel. What they’re lacking in star power, they’ll need to make up for in chemistry. The bench can lift them up through the regular season, but that doesn’t carry over to the playoffs, where it’s best-on-best. If guys are in and out of the lineup with soft tissue issues all season, they’ll never develop the chemistry they need. Kevin Humphreys: My biggest reason for optimism heading into the season is how deep this team is. I understand the shooting limitations that this roster has on paper, but I expect Jalen Green and Dillon Brooks to both take jumps in three-point shooting efficiency this season because they will be taking ‘better’ shots, plus Gillespie and Kennard are snipers. I trust Devin Booker as the Suns’ main playmaker and scorer to win games, and I trust Jordan Ott to configure the rotations to give Booker, Green, and Brooks opportunities to get up shots. Defensively, this team should be one of the best five defenses in the NBA and have the depth to give opposing teams 48 minutes of hellish defense for 82 games. They will force a ton of turnovers, run off misses or makes, and be one of the most fun teams to watch in the NBA this season. CJ Savage: Optimistic about: Has to be seeing what Man Man Maluach can do as a starting (hopefully) center. Close second would be the promise, as yet largely unfulfilled, of Jalen Green. Concerned about the physical and mental decline of Devin Armani Booker. I know he’s said he’s ‘in love’ with basketball again, but what caused him to drop out to begin with? When you are dating the Kardashians and jet-setting, you no longer, IMHO, have basketball/winning a championship/HOF as your primary concern. I think the trajectory now, unless things change for him this season, is that of a former teammate of his, Chris Paul: great player, not quite enough to get a team to the promised land. Mark Bowser: Optimistic about: I do think we’ll see Jordan Ott take a year 2 jump in the head coach role. I often lean on analytics and look at former video coordinators who became head coaches, and at their progression from year 1 to year 2. It’s honestly a mixed bag. But I believe he has the work ethic and intensity to be closer to an Eric Spoelstra (+4 wins) than a James Borrego (-16). I expect better rotations and more emotion at the right moments. Concerned: Inability to sustain injuries or foul problems at the 5 position. I thought this was a strength pre-Mark Williams’ injury. Maluach and Ighodaro are a respectable and complementary pair. If either is unavailable, all the options behind them are marked with question marks. I do not think Huntley or Reath provide enough meaningful rotation minutes, and the small-ball options each have limitations. Where do you land? What are you optimistic about? What concerns you?

stories.title: Nuggets' Julian Strawther to miss opening weeks of NBA season with injury
stories.summary: Denver Nuggets guard Julian Strawther will miss the opening weeks of the 2026-27 season with a left knee sprain.
stories.detailText: Denver Nuggets guard Julian Strawther has been diagnosed with a left knee sprain and is expected to miss the opening weeks of the 2026-27 NBA regular season, including the season opener against the Oklahoma City Thunder on Oct. 22. The team announced that Strawther suffered the injury during a preseason matchup against the Los Angeles Clippers and will be sidelined as he undergoes rehabilitation. Strawther sustained the injury in the third quarter of the game on Oct. 16 when his leg got caught under his body, causing him to bend and land awkwardly. After undergoing an evaluation by the Nuggets' medical staff, it was determined that he had suffered a left knee sprain. Strawther will be re-evaluated in approximately six weeks to determine if he is healthy enough to resume basketball activities. Selected by Denver as the 29th overall pick in the 2023 NBA Draft, Strawther has started 18 games in his career and averaged 7.2 points over 57 appearances last season. stories.title: The Raptors should bring back this blue throwback jersey sooner rather than later
stories.summary: The Huskies should have something to say, if I have any say in it!
stories.detailText: TORONTO, ON - NOVEMBER 12: Raptor the mascot of the Toronto Raptors performs during a break in the action while wearing a throwback Huskies jersey during NBA game action against the New York Knicks at Air Canada Centre on November 12, 2016 in Toronto, Canada. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Tom Szczerbowski/Getty Images) | Getty Images On the 80th anniversary of the 1946-47 Basketball Association of America (BAA) season, the Toronto Raptors get a rare opportunity to mark the occasion of the city’s first professional basketball team. But, unfortunately, they probably won’t take it. The National Basketball Association as we know it has its roots in the BAA, which later went on to merge with the National Basketball League (NBL) in 1949, to create an early version of the NBA . The Association of America had its first game on November 1st, 1946, where the New York Knicks faced off against the Toronto Huskies in the Maple Leaf Gardens. Right there at Church and Carlton, the Huskies lost their first game by two points, ending in a 68-66 loss for Toronto: the team would only play one season in the BAA, collapsing by 1947. But! En-route to making history (and failing soon after), the Huskies established the first brand identity for Torontonian professional basketball. TORONTO, ON – NOVEMBER 12: Raptor the mascot of the Toronto Raptors performs during a break in the action while wearing a throwback Huskies jersey during NBA game action against the New York Knicks at Air Canada Centre on November 12, 2016 in Toronto, Canada. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Tom Szczerbowski/Getty Images) | Getty Images The blue jerseys are striking, bold, and a massive departure from anything the Raptors have done aesthetically in a long time. While taking on the Huskies’ colours is not reinventing the wheel, doing so would be a great callback not only to 80 years since the beginning of the BAA, but to the Raptors’ 2016-17 tribute to the Huskies, and those great years with Lowry and DeRozan. TORONTO, ON – DECEMBER 08: Jonas Valanciunas #17 of the Toronto Raptors tips off against Karl-Anthony Towns #32 of the Minnesota Timberwolves on Huskies night as the Raptors commemorate the Toronto Huskies with throwback jerseys during NBA game action at Air Canada Centre on December 8, 2016 in Toronto, Canada. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement (Photo by Tom Szczerbowski/Getty Images) | Getty Images Who would say no to the idea of a cute, giant dog on the hardwood, at least for a few nights a year? The Raptors have had a somewhat stale brand identity over the years. It seems that the franchise has become allergic to divergence from the red-black-white colour scheme it’s maintained on-and-off for the past 20 years. While there have been reports that the team will, next season, finally rebrand and bring back purple as a part of the team’s visual identity, my heart goes out to the Husky that could have been. It feels like every year, each time has a million jerseys. And the Raptors have maybe two good ones. And that’s being generous. The Huskies have come back before, with the 2009-10 Raptors sporting it, but with Chris Bosh’s departure, so to went the sense of fun from the Raptors’ design choices. Now, are either of the previous jerseys total works of art? I wouldn’t go that far. But, beyond being charming, these jerseys reflect Canada’s role in the history of basketball, something that can be easily ignored. In a league of 30 teams, with 29 of them being American, the Raptors should fight tooth and nail to set themselves apart, and remind their opponents that the basketball league they know and love started right here in the 6ix. The Raptors have not yet announced their City Edition jerseys for this year, and the Husky look would be a perfect fit. But, it is entirely likely that they will choose to take this year to honour the retirement of Kyle Lowry by turning him into a Raptor, and putting that illustration on a city edition jersey. The Raptors have unveiled a Kyle Lowry-themed logo ahead of his jersey retirement this upcoming season 7⃣ (📸: @Raptors ) pic.twitter.com/MUtB7Z1Kpv — Sportsnet (@Sportsnet) August 25, 2026 Cool. Fine. And if it came down to it, nine out of ten times, I’m probably making that call as well. But, every time I think about those jerseys, I remember DeRozan dropping 41 points and whipping the Celtics in them, on a bright blue and white court. And I wish that the Raptors would do a better job commemorating their roots.

(Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last weekend without official NBA content popping up our timelines, folks. Last couple of sleeps before the next time you hit the sack there’s another (or multiple!) new banners hanging from the MSG rafters. Here’s the latest on this beautiful sunny Sunday. Mike Brown tells The Post about how these Knicks will approach this year being the hunted team https://t.co/GKEGMpols2 pic.twitter.com/RSrYn1T89M — New York Post Sports (@nypostsports) October 17, 2026 Mike Brown On delegating responsibilities to his assistant coaches and veteran players: “My coaches can do their job, they can teach, take the lead in the areas that they need to, going by the practice plan and then on top of that, our veteran players, especially with the new guys, they can coach those guys because they kind of got a feel and they kind of know what we’re expecting on both ends of the floor.” On his emotions ahead of the Knicks’ championship ring ceremony and banner raising: “Obviously I’m going to be filled with a lot of different emotions. That’s a special moment. I’m going to be a little selfish, but for me individually, not only that, for my family, for the people in the organization, the team, the players, the other coaches, but just as importantly, the city of New York and the fans of the Knicks all around the world … so to see that happening while knowing the history of it, and knowing how hard it is to let alone get there on top of winning it, it’s going to be an awesome feeling with a ton of emotion inside. We’re all human, the trick is now to really appreciate and enjoy that moment and still try to lock in and get ready for the game and know you got to move forward once it’s over.” On the challenges of defending an NBA championship: “There are a lot of challenges in trying to do that. That’s why it hasn’t happened in the NBA in the last eight, nine years. In all of sports, you don’t hear a ton about back-to-back champions in the modern sports world no matter what sport it is you’re playing. The added quote, unquote pressure that some people may allow to seep in as the year goes on, there could be more jealousies, that the team is not connected, and people forget about sacrificing for the betterment of the team. Everybody has naturally been telling you how great you are the whole summer, and so you think you’re great, and you don’t have to go through and/or embrace the process like you did when you got there the first time because you think you know and it’s just going to happen in moments when you think it needs to happen. There’s a lot that can impact it. “And for me, the biggest thing is trying to make sure our group understands that this is a new season, it’s a new team, and there are new challenges in front of us. Therefore, it’s not about the end result, we have to really make sure we focus our energy and effort on the process, by embracing all the details of the process. And if we do, that’s going to give us our best opportunity to do it again.” On how the Knicks will handle being the hunted team: “That’s another one, everybody likes to play the Knicks anyway, especially in MSG, and now it’s just an added carrot to the whole deal. We have a mature group, and that’s one of the main things that gives me — I don’t know if hope is the right word — but gives me hope that we’re going to take this or embrace this process like no other. I truly believe that the maturity of the group is going to help when it comes to all of it, not just being The Hunted, but handling being patted on the back all year, and media scrutiny that we’re going to be under and pressures of the other things that we’re going to be under. I think that’s what’s going to help a ton.” On Jalen Brunson’s superpower: “His focus and determination.” On OG Anunoby’s superpower: “His potential with his size, his athleticism, and his skillset.” On Karl-Anthony Towns’ superpower: “His skillset and his size.” On Mikal Bridges’ superpower: “His versatility.” On Josh Hart’s superpower: “His ability to connect the group, with sacrifice and determination.” On his expectations for the Knicks’ bench: “I’m excited about it. I’m looking forward to giving guys an opportunity that they might not have gotten before.” On replacing Mitchell Robinson’s contributions following his departure to Boston: “I talked to our guys about this. When I was in Golden State, we had a really good team the year we won back-to-back (2017 and 2018) and KD [Kevin Durant] left after that [after the 2019 season] and everybody thought that, rightfully so, we were going to go into the tank, because you can’t replace KD with one player. In 2022, we won it again, we basically had the same core minus KD. We replaced him basically with a young Jordan Poole, Otto Porter and Andrew Wiggins. And collectively, those three guys plus the rest of the group just brought a little bit more to the table, and we were able to get it done in 2022. So it’s no different with Mitch. Mitch is a great player. We’re not bringing Andre [Drummond] in here to quote, unquote be Mitch. Andre’s going to be Andre, but that means everybody else has to give a little bit more defensively, and has to give a little bit more when it comes to offensive and defensive rebounding,” On the Knicks fans and how New York celebrates its championship teams: “It’s like no other. This is my fifth championship that I’ve been a part of in some really good cities. “Love you guys, love your energy. Keep bringing it, because we’re looking forward to having another fun year.” Soon it will go to the rafters 🔊 pic.twitter.com/koAapSZjVW — New York Basketball (@NBA_NewYork) October 18, 2026 Mikal Bridges On the improved Eastern Conference and increased competition: “You see what goes on. A lot of teams got better, and it’s good. Excited for all of the other teams; you love when the competition’s high. Who doesn’t love that?” Andre Drummond On developing his jump shot throughout his NBA career: “I did it when no one was watching. … So here we are, 15 years later, s–t, better late than never, right?” On the skills that have allowed him to remain in the NBA entering his 15th season: “Be a master of what I do. I mean, I’m able to rebound the ball at a high clip still. Obviously with the addition of the three-point shot, being able to be a good pick-and-roll defender, and just a great locker room guy altogether is really what keeps me around.” On his passing ability and how his game has evolved: “I love to pass, I love to see the floor, and I play well in the pocket. … The game is changing, [my] guards like to score, and I throw the pocket pass in.” Jalen Brunson On Andre Drummond establishing his own identity rather than replacing Mitchell Robinson: “not coming in to be Mitch, he’s coming in to be himself.” On Mike Brown taking time to build a personal relationship with him: “He came down to Jersey in the summer, and we sat, had dinner, talked for two-and-a-half, three hours, whatever, and did not talk about basketball or what we were gonna do. So that just tells you who he is. That’s a genuine dude, and he just wanted to get to know all of us before we got into our jobs and to see what we had to do as a team. But it’s just genuinely who he is.” “I want y’all to know I’m ready for y’all. Y’all not ready for me, I’m applying all pressure on y’all all summer…Y’all was sleeping on me…All gas no brakes-that’s gone be me rest of my life” — Dink Pate’s 12 straight for Westchester wins last game of year, Mark Pope courtside pic.twitter.com/RP4ZHvJrfo — New York Basketball (@NBA_NewYork) March 29, 2026 Karl-Anthony Towns On Mike Brown addressing the team’s personal struggles and contract uncertainty: “Mike talked about mindfulness. He talked about the situation to all of us openly, and we all talked as a team, as a family — the coaches and players — and it’s still so amazing to see how connected this team is, to see how much of a family unit we really are. “It was really cool to have a coach talk to us about being you, about the struggles in life, and us being together and understanding where everyone is in life and the situations they deal with as a family, as brothers, that will allow us to even be more connected and allows us to even be a better team. That was an amazing job by him as our leader to approach the elephant in the room and to allow us, the players and the coaches and the ones who are on that core into Game 4, Game 5, who really found a way to get this title back to New York, allowing us to be human.” Josh Hart On Andre Drummond’s skill set: “Way better passing than I thought he was.” On Mike Brown’s leadership style and personality: “Honestly, I didn’t know he was a military baby until you said it. Obviously, he’s someone who commands attention and respect and those kinds of things.” “Now, he’s super chill. He’s a great person, lets us know, holds us accountable when we’re out there not doing what we’re supposed to do. “He’s more of a ‘Who let the dogs out’ kind of guy.” Miles McBride's agent leaves door open for future talks with Knicks https://t.co/FKQImYLilV pic.twitter.com/CL5HNTvc4Z — New York Post Sports (@nypostsports) October 18, 2026 Mark Bartelstein (Deuce McBride’s Agent) On McBride’s desire for a contract extension and the possibility of future negotiations: “No doubt, he would love to get that. But at the end of the day, you work for the Knicks and it takes two sides to get a deal done. And if the Knicks aren’t ready to do extensions right now, then we just gotta buckle up and go have a great season. He’ll be a free agent this summer, but we’ll see. We’ve got a great relationship with [president] Leon [Rose] and the front office. We’ll see: there may be opportunities during the season, maybe in the near future. Who knows where we’ll be able to have those conversations.” On McBride’s contributions to the Knicks and his willingness to play through injury: “We’ve spoken to the Knicks throughout the summer. Miles, like any player in his position, would love to get an extension. I think he’s earned it. He’s been a huge part of where that organization has gone over the last three or four years. He’s been their sixth man. A lot of people don’t realize how hurt he played last year in the playoffs. He had abdominal surgery that caused him to miss a couple of months. He came back and he wasn’t really right yet, but he didn’t want to miss the opportunity to be there for his teammates.” Joel Embiid, on facing the Knicks on opening night: "I don't really feel like watching that whole ceremony, so I guess I'll be in the locker room." "It's the first game…The way I see it is taking it day-by-day, slowing getting better…It's about the process that it takes to… pic.twitter.com/tdExscxMlX — PHLY Sixers (@PHLY_Sixers) October 17, 2026 Joel Embiid On whether he will watch the Knicks’ championship ceremony before the 76ers’ season opener: “I don’t really feel like watching that whole ceremony. I guess I’ll be in the locker room.” Jaylen Brown On facing the Knicks on opening night during their championship celebration: “It’s an honor. Opening night, it’s primetime, the former champions, I think it’s serendipitous.” Kendrick Perkins tells The Post how Mike Brown can best navigate the Knicks' Karl-Anthony Towns contract drama https://t.co/fAiSgvzbSk pic.twitter.com/VGC0SS02WU — New York Post Sports (@nypostsports) October 17, 2026 Kendrick Perkins On the Philadelphia 76ers being the biggest threat to the Knicks in the Eastern Conference: “The East has caught up with the West. You have the 76ers, obviously, you have the Toronto Raptors, you have Giannis [Antetokounmpo] with Miami, I think they’re still a few pieces away. But to me, if I had to pick one, it would be the 76ers. Nick Nurse won a championship [as coach of the Raptors in 2019]. Nick Nurse had to figure how pieces worked when he was in Toronto. And when you have guys that have high IQs — Jaylen Brown is a Finals MVP, LeBron James is [not just] arguably the greatest player but one of the smartest players to play the game of basketball. That’s not going to be a hard adjustment. … Offensively I see them getting out and running. I could see them being probably the best transition team offensively in the league. But I also could see them figuring things out on the fly while they’re still winning games during the regular season. And I also see LeBron James bringing out the best in Joel Embiid.” On how Mike Brown should handle Karl-Anthony Towns’ contract situation: “KAT is an emotional guy. And if I’m Mike Brown, the biggest thing is from a personal side, I would just want Towns to know that he’s loved on a day-to-day basis. That don’t mean that there’s not going to be times where you have to call him out in film, but if I’m Mike Brown, I’d go the extra mile to extend my love, whether that’s on the road, him meeting him for breakfast before shootaround, maybe dinners, just to let him know his value. And to let him know that he’s a huge and the most important part of this team. … It would be through actions and less through words.” On the challenges of defending an NBA championship: “The first thing is health, obviously. The second thing is getting through the regular season knowing that everywhere in every game that you play, you’re going to get everyone’s best shot. But last but not least is having everyone continue to lose themselves in the team and play agenda-free basketball. Because what ends up happening is when you win a championship, because of the praise that you get in the offseason, everyone starts to believe that they were the reason and guys come back and want a bigger role, instead of staying and playing and being a star of that role that helped them win the championship.” On Jalen Brunson’s development into an elite player and leader: “Offensively, I believe that Jalen Brunson over the last three years before Giannis was injured, has been consistently the best player in the Eastern Conference. But last year we saw him take that leap of accountability. We saw him doing the little things of fighting to get over screens. We saw him doing things of getting back in transition and getting extra possessions by taking charges. We saw him take over a Game 4 in Madison Square Garden in the second half to direct traffic and get buckets. We just saw leadership, right? We saw a guy in probably the hardest market to play in, have composure, have leadership and be able to perform on the biggest moments. But I think the most important thing is that he accepted the challenge of actually playing defense and playing enough defense where he wasn’t a liability. But also playing defense where the Spurs couldn’t hunt him out on the big stage. … He’s one of if not my favorite players in the NBA, but history tells us that we haven’t had a back-to-back champion in the last 8-9 years.” Piccolo pulled up to the France riots 😭😭 pic.twitter.com/M4S5Iz8hgd — vids that go hard (@vidsthatgohard) October 17, 2026

stories.title: PTH Roundtable: biggest impact from a new player?
stories.summary: Most impactful newcomer?
stories.detailText: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - OCTOBER 10: Pascal Siakam #43 of the Indiana Pacers dribbles against Luguentz Dort #0 of the Atlanta Hawks at Gainbridge Fieldhouse on October 10, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images This is the first of a series of roundtable questions I’m asking the staff here at Peachtree Hoops about the Hawks this upcoming season. The first question: which newly acquired player will have the biggest impact for the Hawks this season? Wes: I think Luguentz Dort will bring a level of toughness, defensive versatility, and an ability to play his role on offense that the team desperately needed. Now that the reins are in the hands of Jalen Johnson to run the show, Dort will fit in as a corner three-point shooter who has tons of experience operating around a star player. But clearly, defensively is where he’ll make his name. He’s a bigger body than even all-world defender Dyson Daniels, so he, Daniels and Nickeil Alexander-Walker can share the load of taking on the other team’s best perimeter player depending on the night. Malik: I’ll have to agree and say and say Lu Dort. I think he was the biggest addition to the team this offseason, and it’s because of what he brings to the defensive side of the ball. He’s going to make life easier for Dyson Daniels, and he could guard almost every position on the floor. The Hawks’ defense was good last season, but it’s going to be even better with Dort in the fold. It’s also hard not to mention the championship experience he’ll bring to the team. That will go a long way for a team that’s looking to be contenders. Garrett: Luguentz Dort. To me, he was Onsi Saleh’s biggest addition this offseason. The Knicks exposed Atlanta’s struggles with physicality in the playoffs, and Dort directly addresses that issue. He’s one of the league’s best defenders, embraces tough assignments and knows what it takes to win in the postseason. That combination is a major plus for a Hawks team looking to take the next step. Graham : I really like the deal to acquire Aaron Wiggins, I think he’ll have more of a positive impact than expected, but it’s hard to overlook just what Lu Dort is going to bring. It’s not just what Dort brings – which I’ll discuss in a moment – but the commitment the Hawks have made stylistically, and philosophically. Dort’s shooting struggles in the postseason are well documented, as are those of Dyson Daniels. It’s going to be difficult to have both of those players out in crunch-time, but on the defensive end of the ball the Hawks have made a clear commitment to a defensive mentality. Now, Dort can be included into ‘chaos’ lineups which can involve Nickeil Alexander-Walker, Daniels, Dort, Johnson, and Okongwu – every single one of those players can hold their own defensively and excel (Johnson is more than capable of this when he applies himself to do so). The Hawks may have an offensive ceiling with Daniels and Dort on the floor, but they have the defense to still bring a net rating in those scenarios. If Dort and Daniels can improve their three-point shooting and sustain it in the postseason, then the ceiling is removed for this squad. With Dort, the Hawks can have at least two plus defensive wings on at all times. The versatility he provides to what the Hawks can now run out on the court lineup-wise is a big step forward. Dort himself will bring a toughness, a mentality that the Hawks will thrive off of, and championship experience to learn from. Everything Dort brings will only help Atlanta grow on and off the court as they try to take the next step; Dort is the perfect acquisition for the Hawks’ next phase of their journey. The message is clear: it’s defense first.

stories.title: “I don’t care if the shot is gonna fall or not.” Darko Rajaković thinks Allen Graves should let it fly
stories.summary: The coach stood by the rookie’s performance in the preseason, praising and supporting the forward
stories.detailText: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 16: Allen Graves #22 of the Toronto Raptors goes up for a layup against John Collins #20 of the Detroit Pistons during the third quarter of a preseason game at Little Caesars Arena on October 16, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Mike Mulholland/Getty Images) | Getty Images Allen Graves has had a bit of a rough outing in the Raptors’ preseason games, but his coach sees things as going all according to plan. In two games played, the forward has averaged just over 19 minutes of playing time, posting numbers of seven points, five and a half rebounds, and an assist and a steal a-piece per game. Less than stellar from a first round pick, especially considering that the scoring is being done at a clip of 25% accuracy, while shooting just over nine percent from three. Offensively, Graves has struggled, especially in his last game, where he was four for thirteen, and missed all five shots from three. However, the rookie can’t be faulted for what he’s doing: after all, he’s just following his coach’s directions. On the 14th of October, Darko Rajaković was asked about Allen Graves’ feel for the game despite his inaccuracy (the night before, the forward had shot 16% from three). The coach’s response? DETROIT, MI – OCTOBER 16: Allen Graves #22 of the Toronto Raptors shoots the ball during the game against the Detroit Pistons during a preseason game on October 16, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Chris Schwegler/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images “I don’t care if the shot is gonna fall or not.” “He’s a great shooter,” Rajaković continued, intently. “I promise him this morning, the first time when I see him, that he does not take open shot when I see him, I’m going to sit him on the bench. It’s going to be simple as that.” It’s this type of confidence and championing of his players that has characterized Rajaković‘s tenure as the Raptors’ head coach. This type of leadership and standing by players who are down can be instrumental in keeping a locker room united, but at the same time, the coach is not simply making a leap of blind faith. “He’s a great shooter,” repeated Rajaković, as if drilling a lesson into schoolchildren who were liable to forget if not reminded. “He has a great feel for the game and yesterday was a typical rookie game playing for the first time in front of home crowd. That was such a typical game, I was so happy for him to get in a foul trouble, to miss shots, and I think that was awesome.” It is this clear willingness to let a player develop that is a big part of what sets the Raptors apart as an organization. A few rough preseason games aren’t something to be ashamed of, in the mind of Darko Rajaković. They’re a learning experience, and more than that, a milestone for a young player. Showing flashes of greatness on the court are not being prioritized over working on oneself — yet. It seems for now, Allen Graves will be given the room to make mistakes, to brick jumpshots, and take all the missteps that one might take in an NBA game, in the service of maturing into a well-rounded player. It would be nice if everyone was afforded the luxury of time and external validation that seems to be happening here. But, even if that can’t be the case, it’s good to know that some NBA coaches have real heart. It seems that Rajaković was channelling his inner Dion Waiters when he spoke to the media last week. More Waiters: "I’d rather go 0 for 30 than 0 for 9 because you go 0 for 9 that means you stopped shooting.That means you lost confidence." — Shandel Richardson (@ShandelRich) January 31, 2017 Maybe Waiters, and Rajaković, are both right. Let’s make sure that Graves doesn’t lose confidence.

stories.title: Lakers experience ‘growing pains’ in first look with Big 3
stories.summary: How did the Lakers look with their "Big 3" on the court?
stories.detailText: After multiple weeks of waiting, the Lakers were finally able to see what it looked like when their Big 3 was on the floor together. The results made it clear there’s plenty of room for growth. With Luka Doncic, Austin Reaves and Walker Kessler available for Friday’s preseason finale loss to the Nuggets on Friday night at Crypto.com Arena, the wait to see how the team would look with its most consequential players alongside each other ended. The Lakers finally got a look at their “Big 3, which includes Luka Doncic (77) and Walker Kessler (14). NBAE via Getty Images Finally, the highly anticipated Doncic-Kessler pick and roll would be unleashed on an opposing team instead of held within the confines of the team’s practice floor. The 7-foot-2 center, who made his debut in Tuesday’s loss to the Warriors in Las Vegas, would be able to build off his first NBA game in nearly a year in a positive way and complement both of the team’s star guards. And the Lakers’ wing defenders — this time with Matisse Thybulle and Ziaire Williams in the first unit in what could be a preview for the regular-season opener against the Warriors — would have their defensive anchor behind them, allowing them to be more aggressive with their perimeter defense. Some of this came to fruition. Luka Doncic (77) was responsible for five of the Lakers’ 10 first-half turnovers. NBAE via Getty Images But other aspects left a lot to be desired. The biggest among them: too many early turnovers, with the Lakers recording six giveaways by the end of the first quarter and 10 turnovers by the middle of the second. It was evident that Kessler was adjusting to what his new life will look like when defenses load up on Doncic and Reaves, and the playmaking responsibilities that’ll come in those moments. “There’s going to be some growing pains, just lack of reps together so far,” Reaves said. “More than likely going to pick up on it sooner than later. So we’ll continue to grow that over the next couple days and be ready for Opening Night.” The growing pains didn’t take away from the good the Lakers were able to accomplish. Lakers star guard Austin Reaves (15) also struggled to take care of the ball in the team’s preseason finale. NBAE via Getty Images Sandro Mamukelashvili and Williams showed immediate connections with Doncic. Kessler was able to get a better idea of what his life will look like in the short roll when Doncic and Reaves are blitzed in the pick and roll — a strategy that the Nuggets deployed early and often against the Lakers. “Obviously there’s a transitional period playing with both Luka and AR on the floor together,” Kessler said. “Kind of what I was saying before, about the blitz and ball screens and playing out of that pocket. I started to get it a little bit. Obviously Luka and AR are pretty used to that.” The hiccups on Friday made it even more apparent how helpful it would’ve been for the Lakers to get more reps with their Big 3 on the court together. How certain rhythms and cadences can only be understood when players are on the court together against another team. Coach JJ Redick made it clear his team will be ready to go when the games start to matter in the standings when they kick off the regular season against the Warriors on Wednesday. Friday will be an important part in making sure Redick is correct. stories.title: Den Questions: Start of the AntBall Era
stories.summary: A few questions for the Wolves first 10 games of the 2026-27 season.
stories.detailText: Welcome to the Den! Over the course of the season I want to take 10 game snap shots and ask and answer a few questions about the Wolves. Some of these questions are about serious hoop, some of them are the silly questions I think about riding the Green Line to the Target Center. So curl up with a beverage of your choice, get comfy, and stay awhile. 1. Are Ant and LaMelo better together? If we can take anything from preseason (we shouldn’t), and if head coach Chris Finch is giving us any hints to his plan for the season in his quotes about lineups (he isn’t), then Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball will share the floor a lot. The reasons to keep them separated are obvious. Both players can handle the ball. Both players have tremendous gravity on offense creating opportunities for others. The Wolves have a dearth of ball handling and keeping someone on the court at all times who won’t get bullied in a full-court press is imperative. So why would Finch ever play a minute without one of his star guards on the court? Well… Overwhelming Offense: With both guards on the court, they create a Sophie’s Choice for how to guard the Wolves that leads to easy mismatches easily exploitable with Ant’s athleticism or Ball’s passing. If both players are loaded up on, there are plenty of other players to kick the ball to for easy looks. Bench Strengths: Fresh off Terrance Shannon Jr.’s impressive 2026 playoff performance, Finch noted the need to put the ball in his hands to get the most out of him. Ball or Edwards might play well alongside TJ by spotting up for threes as Shannon barrels to the hoop and collapses the defense. That said, both players are better when their usage is higher and the Wolves have other bench shooters that TJ can feed. Establishing Roles: Melo knows his primary role. Its the one role he has always known. He is there to stir the drink on offense and get everyone involved. Ant is going back to his best role as a shooting guard. He will move off-ball and create advantages for his team. On the defensive side of things, Ant will need to establish himself on defense and that will be easier when he is not the primary creator. There will be moments in games where the pair are split up. Ant will likely play more minutes than Melo. To get the most out of both players skillsets, those times apart should be limited. 2. What is Joan’s good/bad ratio? As reported by Jace Frederick of The Pioneer Press during the short tenure of Rob Dillingham, head coach Chris Finch said of Dillingham, “If you play three games, you hope that you get one good, one not so good, and one maybe stinker. And you got to turn that into two positives and maybe one negative. Once we get there, then things start to go.” If Finch is holding Joan to a similar standard, how many bad games can the Wolves withstand for every good game Joan provides. I believe the Wolves can weather two bad games for every one that impresses. For all the talk of a team focused on defense, this is a team built to score in bunches. There will be games where defense is wanting any minute Rudy Gobert is off the floor. So long as the offense is humming and it should be, then the Wolves can handle Joan riding the pine on account of leading the league in fouls. The second year player needs minutes and needs opportunities to make mistakes and learn from them. The bench defense does rely on him, but this is a team that will win with their offense as they learn and adapt to a leaner and smaller team. 3. How many minutes should Melo average? In his six-year NBA tenure, LaMelo Ball has only played 61% of games. Much of that was due to injury, some of that was due to being on a team in the tank for a better lottery pick. He has played over 50 games in a season three times. Last season was his second most games played. He also played his fewest average minutes per game at 28 minutes. The early preseason returns, such as they can be relied on, have shown how dynamic the Wolves can be with Ball on the floor. It will be imperative for Coach Finch to go against his nature of leaning on his starters. The Wolves do have a bevy of guards to slot into the starting spot should Melo miss a few games but none of them offer the dynamism of size, dribbling, shooting, and passing. To keep LaMelo available while also getting the most out of him, I look to the Wolves former floor general Mike Conley in the 2024 season. At 29 minutes a game, the 36-year-old guard was able to suit up for 76 games. If Ball plays over 70 games the Wolves will be in contention for a top four seed in the playoffs. 4. How long can effort outlast physicality? Everyone is talking about it: the Wolves got smaller this season. With Naz Reid, Julius Randle, Mike Conley, Kyle Anderson, and Joe Ingles all playing elsewhere, the Wolves lost just under 32 feet and 11 inches of height. Minnesota added Melo, Jonathan Kuminga, Trey Lyles, Cody Williams, and Isaiah Evans for a total of 33 feet and one inch of height. Unfortunately this pedantic look doesn’t actually dispel the fact that the Wolves are not as big as their rivals and will need to be creative to counteract this discrepancy. Mostly they will rely on effort in the hopes that sweat equity will overtake size. And it is here that I have my biggest concern for the year. In the early parts of the season, as teams are trying to figure themselves out and miscommunications are more common, this effort strategy has a better chance of working. In the bleak mid-winter especially with the new anti-tanking rules in place, that effort will be harder to summon and the size issue will still be there. I don’t foresee a trade unless the Wolves are dealing away one of their cheaper contracts and that likely doesn’t bring back much of a needle mover. No amount of weight room work is going to build the requisite muscle in time for it to be of use. Minnesota will need to get clever in their defense to earn the extra possessions that decide close games. An option could be found in gambling for more steals at the risk of drawing fouls. Per Stat Muse the Detroit Pistons were called for the most fouls last year while also forcing the most turnovers . This style of play led to the third best point differential for the season last year behind the Oklahoma City Thunder and the San Antonio Spurs . The Wolves fouled the third most last season while only forcing the 12th most turnovers. In a league trending bigger, general manager Tim Connelly gambled on smaller players. Those players will need to take similar risks to earn extra possessions when the effort to rebound runs into a bigger and stronger wall. 5. Which Wolf Takes the Leap? Ant, Melo, Rudy Gobert, and Jaden McDaniels all have accolades in their trophy case. There are things each of them could do to improve. McDaniels could move into All-Star territory, though with Ant and Ball on the team, barring the Wolves holding the number one seed, I don’t see them getting three all-stars. Melo could join Ant in the All-NBA space in a best of all worlds eventuality for the Wolves. Ant could win MVP, the pinnacle of the league. The likely leaper candidates are Jonathan Kuminga, Ayo Dosunmu, Joan Beringer, Terrance Shannon Jr. Kuminga’s Case : I will keep beating this drum until he proves otherwise. Kuminga needs to model his game after Josh Hart. He won’t win Most Improved Player, but he will win a decade plus career. Sixth Man Ayo : Posting one of four triple doubles for the Wolves last year and scoring 43 points off the bench in the playoffs when Ant and Donte DiVincenzo were injured, Dosunmu showed the ability to morph into whatever player his team needed. If he can find consistency while maintaining this doppelganger, he’ll put himself solidly into the Sixth Man of the Year race and likely the Most Improved Player race. Go On Joan : If Joan can keep his fouling to below four a game and increase his rebounding to six or more a game, up from his 2.3 average now, then they Wolves have answered one of their biggest concerns. This leap would likely only be seen amongst the Minnesota faithful and deep NBA stat head sickos. TJ Gets a Payday : TJ is on the cusp of a contract extension. For him to earn a payday he will need to win his minutes. Whether that is by scoring, setting up his teammates, or using his leaping ability and size to grab defensive rebounds to end possessions, TJ’s next contract appears directly tied to his EPM for this season. My bet is on Ayo who has the most versatility. 6. Which Wolf has the Dunk of the Year? I wish this could be Joan because of how angrily he dunks, but there are few dunks by big men who make the cut for Dunk of the Year. Shaquille O’Neal dunking Chris Dudley to the floor and DeAndre Jordan’s alley-oop dunk over Brandon Knight are top of mind and beyond that a struggle unless the backboard is shattered. Dunks of the Year belong to the players who break the bonds of gravity to violently flush it through the rim. The three most likely candidates for the Wolves are Ant, Kuminga, or TJ. TJ treats the rim like it pulled up Urban Dictionary and started listing derogatory terms to describe his mother. He has the speed and leaping ability to capture the imagination. Very strong candidate. Kuminga has listened to years of criticism about his deficiencies and has watched his annual earnings drop back to below what he made on the third year of his rookie contract. With a team looking to set him up, if he puts all of his frustration at Steve Kerr, the national media, and maybe his agent into a single dunk, we might see the backboard shatter. Ant has the greatest advantage of name recognition and a highlight reel worth of past DOTY finalists. Given the popularity of the Wolves backcourt, if he posterizes an opponent off a Melo alley-oop then… View Link 7. Which Wolf gets a new nationally recognized nickname? According to Basketball Reference these are the nicknames for the Wolves likely nine man rotation. In bold after them, I have added a few of my thoughts for consideration. LaMelo Ball: Melo – LaFrench Connection LaFrench is his middle name Anthony Edwards: Ant, Ant-Man – Ripley for when he defeats “the Alien” Victor Wembenyama . Jaden McDaniels: Seatbelt, Big Mac, Slim – Sith Lord already sort of out there with the Darth Jaden Memes , The Warden ( puts people in cells + Game of Thrones Warden of the North tie-ins . Jonathan Kuminga: none listed – DR3 a play on where Kuminga is from, the Democratic Republic of the Congo aka the DRC, heavily contingent on him becoming a + three point shooter . Rudy Gobert: The Stifle Tower, The French Rejection, The Gobert Report, Gobzilla, Big Ru – Rudy has plenty and I don’t think I can do any better. Quamdeen Ayopo “Ayo” Dosunmu: none listed – Ayo is already too good. It has a singularity to it, it is easy to yell, and conjures both someone grabbing your attention while asking you, “what’s up?” (For clarity, his name is pronounced “EYE-o”) Terrence Shannon Jr.: none listed – Southpaw I don’t know if his right hand will ever be reliable. Joan Berringer: none listed – The Baron of Blocks much as I love Baron J, I don’t see much of a jump shot emerging Trey Lyles: TreyMamba – Spanish Honeymaker because he played for a Spanish team last year and you know, el bees, as in this team is twiggy up and down and Finch is gonna need to add some pounds to some lineups For my money, I think McDaniels is primed for a nationally recognized nickname. Clyde Frazier was calling him Mac during the recent Wolves versus Knicks bout. While a few on this list do not have any and Jaden has three, none are called out with the type of exuberance that leads to water cooler talk where he is spoken about only in nickname. 8. Is this The Year? In a word… PARIS, FRANCE – AUGUST 10: Anthony Edwards #5 of Team USA smiles after receiving a gold medal during the Men's Gold Medal Game on August 10, 2024 at the AccorHotels Arena in Paris, France. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2024 NBAE (Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images No. I think the Wolves are going to be a very good team. I think they have a better than 50% chance to be in the top four of the Western Conference. I even think they could surprise the world and beat one of San Antonio or Oklahoma City and make it to the Western Conference Finals. I do not think they are good enough to beat both of those teams if all are healthy. All that said… HOWL! 82-0! Hope springs eternal! 9. Where are we in the Marathon? While basketball was the first sport I fell in love with, distance running was the first sport I was actually good at. I have run a few marathons and given the grind of an 82-game season, I wanted to take a look at where the Wolves are in the grand scheme of the most famous distance race. The Wolves are wrapping up preseason which equates to the final week before the race. The energy is high, there is a touch of nervousness, mileage and workouts are not maxing out the legs or lungs. The Wolves’ regular season rotations aren’t playing in all of the games, and the deep bench are getting more run than they normally would. In those final days before the race there is a mix of feeling incredible, muscles are relaxed with a spring in your step. Other days any small twinge can feel like a five alarm fire that your body isn’t ready. The starting lineup makes sense. With Jaden at the point of attack and Rudy minding the hoop, Ant, Ball, and Kuminga are showing the effort needed to force stops. On the other side of the court, the ball is moving more than any Wolves offense in recent memory. Opposing defenses are struggling deciding which player to concede a shot from. Even still, it is a long season and injuries are sure to creep up and sap some of the strength of the team. On the bench there are bright spots but an equal number of worries, some already mentioned in this article. Can Joan keep his hands to himself enough to stay on the court? Should so much of the point guard duties be foisted upon TJ’s left hand? Is there a more glaring reason Trey Lyles spent a year out of the league? None of these things will be known until the games start mattering and the minute distribution comes into alignment. At this point, there isn’t much left for Connelly, Finch, or the rest of the Wolves players to do but get to opening day ready and healthy. Anxiety and excitement grows with each passing day until the starting gun fires and all the worry melts away and you have to contend with the course in front of you. One step at a time. 10. Wolves Record Through Ten The Wolves first ten games are filled with hard-nosed defensive teams. The Giannis and Bam Heat, the Magic, the Raptors , the Cavaliers , the Rockets and the Spurs. If they can go 50-50 in that stretch, they have the talent to dispatch the Warriors , Clippers, Bucks and Pelicans. Wolves start the season 7-3. Canis Comment Section: What questions do you have? How would you answer any of the these questions?

IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect 2. New York Knicks We underestimated the Knicks last season and won’t repeat that mistake. They return 10 of their 12 rotational players. They’ve proven that no deficit fazes them. And Jalen Brunson is fearless. 3. Oklahoma City Thunder The 2025 championship Thunder were stunned by the Spurs in the Western Conference finals last season. This roster is deep, young, talented and hungry to get back atop the league. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, who has won two straight MVP awards, isn’t going to take his foot off the gas this season. 4. Philadelphia 76ers LeBron James, Jaylen Brown, Joel Embiid and Tyrese Maxey? This should be fun. It might take them a second to figure things out and develop chemistry. But if they do, watch out . It’ll be interesting to see if this superteam takes over the league or flames out, such as the disappointing Nets who never got past the second round of the playoffs despite having Kevin Durant, Kyrie Irving and James Harden on the roster. Philadelphia 76ers’ LeBron James dribbles during the second half of a preseason NBA basketball game against the Boston Celtics, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026, in Philadelphia. AP Photo/Matt Slocum 5. Cleveland Cavaliers The regular season doesn’t matter for this Cavs team. They keep combusting in the playoffs, including getting swept by the Knicks in the 2026 Eastern Conference finals. Either they make a deep run with Donovan Mitchell, Harden, Peyton Watson and Evan Mobley or else it’s hard to imagine there isn’t going to be a reckoning soon. 6. Los Angeles Lakers This team has a lot of question marks. But also a lot of potential . If Luka Doncic, Austin Reaves and Walker Kessler play to their potential and the team’s perimeter defense surpasses expectations, the Lakers could be very good. But this team has nine new players, including Kessler, who played only five games last season after having season-ending shoulder surgery. So, yeah, lots of questions. Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic (77) shoots during pregame warmups before a game against the Denver Nuggets at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, California, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect 7. Houston Rockets Fred VanVleet has returned after missing last season because a torn ACL and meniscus in his right knee that he suffered in an offseason workout in September 2025. Alperen Sengun is looking good. Durant is still very much Durant. This team could be the dark horse of the West. 8. Indiana Pacers Didn’t you learn not to overlook Tyrese Haliburton back in 2025? You know, when he stunned the NBA by leading the Pacers to the NBA Finals before suffering a torn Achilles tendon in Game 7 of that series? Sure, he’s going to be shaking off rust this season. But he’s someone to keep your eye on. 9. Detroit Pistons The Pistons added more scoring threats after Cade Cunningham and Jalen Duren were overcrowded by defenders in the paint last postseason. If Ausar Thompson can also be counted on having a reliable outside shot, they could be good. 10. Minnesota Timberwolves The Timberwolves’ ceiling rose after they acquired LaMelo Ball, pairing him with Anthony Edwards, Rudy Gobert and Jaden McDaniels. Jonathan Kuminga was another great addition to the roster. If the hype is real, the Timberwolves could give the top teams in the West a run for their money. 11. Boston Celtics Brown is gone. We’re going to see what Jayson Tatum can do without his longtime counterpart, with whom he won a championship in 2024. And this should be a revenge season of sorts for Paul George, who caught a lot of strays from pundits amid the Brown trade. 12. Denver Nuggets The Nuggets had an underwhelming offseason. But any team with Nikola Jokic is going to be in the championship hunt. Their starting five of Joker, Jamal Murray, Aaron Gordon, Cameron Johnson and Christian Braun is very skilled, but their lack of depth could haunt them. 13. Miami Heat Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo are going to be a lot of fun on both sides of the court. This team should be a title threat in the next couple of years. 14. Toronto Raptors Kawhi Leonard has returned to the Raptors, whom he carried to a championship in 2019. After far too many injury-riddled seasons with the Clippers, he looked great last year, averaging 27.9 points on 50.5% shooting, 6.4 rebounds, 3.6 assists and 1.9 steals per game over 65 contests. When he’s healthy, he’s one of the league’s best players. 15. Dallas Mavericks Cooper Flagg is gearing up for a breakout season, and Irving is returning to the lineup after missing last season because of torn left ACL. It’ll be interesting to see what new coach Dusty May can do with this group in the wake of the Doncic-Anthony Davis debacle. 16. Orlando Magic Paolo Banchero, Franz Wagner and Jalen Suggs are formidable, but a lot of questions remain around this team, especially with its outside shooting. Their eye-popping payroll coupled with the fact that this team hasn’t gotten past the first round of the playoffs the last three years means they’re on a very short rope to figure things out quickly. 17. Atlanta Hawks This team should have a strong defense behind Lu Dort and Dyson Daniels. If Jalen Johnson can continue to take leaps, this team could make some noise. 18. Golden State Warriors The Warriors didn’t have the offseason they hoped. Antetokounmpo was traded to Miami. James chose the 76ers. But if Jimmy Butler returns healthy in a few months from his torn right ACL, he, Steph Curry and Draymond Green could make some noise in the West, especially if Yaxel Lendeborg keeps impressing. 19. Utah Jazz This team is lacking frontcourt depth at the start of the season after Jusuf Nurkic suffered a partial plantar plate tear in the second toe of his right foot during the preseason. But Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson are exciting, and Darryn Peterson could be a difference-maker. 20. Washington Wizards Trae Young and Davis both feel as though they have a lot to prove. Young’s star has fallen. Davis has been on a wild downswing ever since he was dealt to the Mavericks for Doncic. Those two guys should be very fun to track this season as they seek revenge. 21. Los Angeles Clippers This team is down in the dumps following the Aspiration scandal. They’ve hit rock bottom. They’re racked with injuries. But don’t be surprised if coach Tyronn Lue somehow brings out the best in them. 22. Phoenix Suns Devin Booker really needs a great year following last season’s subpar performance. He shot 45.6% from the field, his lowest percentage since his third season in the league. If he can reemerge as a superstar, he and Dillon Brooks could be fun. 23. Portland Trail Blazers This team could be ranked much higher. It depends how Damian Lillard looks after missing last season because of a torn Achilles tendon. And how quickly Lillard, Deni Avdija and Ja Morant can develop a rhythm. There’s a lot of wild cards here. But this team also has the potential to skyrocket in these rankings very soon. 24. Chicago Bulls Caleb Wilson should compete for Rookie of the Year. Josh Giddey is always fun. And Matas Buzelis made leaps last season. The Bulls have a lot of growing to do. But there’s also intrigue here. 25. New Orleans Pelicans We’re entering this season with the same tired storyline. The Pelicans won 26 games last season, yet they refused to pull the plug. Don’t expect much to change this time around. 26. Memphis Grizzlies Cameron Boozer is living up to the hype. He joins some young hotshots in Cedric Coward, Zach Edey, Jaylen Wells and Cam Spencer. This team should be fun. But it’ll be a while before it can make noise. 27. Charlotte Hornets Ball is out. Let’s see what the team’s creators can do without him, especially Brandon Miller, Kon Knueppel, Coby White and Naz Reid. 28. Sacramento Kings Darius Acuff is an electric scorer, and if he lives up to his potential, this team could be worth monitoring. Domantas Sabonis claims he’s healthy following knee surgery. And there’s also always intrigue around Ben Simmons. But winning games is another issue altogether. 29. Brooklyn Nets While everyone suspects the Timberwolves of taking veiled shots at Julius Randle, he could raise the Nets’ ceiling. But it’s a very low ceiling, despite Michael Porter Jr. and Mikel Brown Jr. being on the roster. 30. Milwaukee Bucks Welp, at least the Bucks won a championship in 2021 before everything fell apart.

stories.title: Preseason lessons learned
stories.summary: The preseason has come to an end for the Celtics so here are some things I learned.
stories.detailText: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 16: Jaylen Brown #7 of the Philadelphia 76ers guards Hugo Gonzalez #28 of the Boston Celtics in the third quarter during the preseason game at Xfinity Mobile Arena on October 16, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The Celtics defeated the 76ers 125-120 in overtime. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images The preseason is over so here are ten things that we learned about the 2026-27 Celtics in the preseason. 1. Jayson Tatum is all the way back The return of Jayson Tatum was a success last year. The end was disappointing, but for him to look as good as he did that early off of the torn Achilles was a big deal for him and the Celtics. This season is about getting back to peak Jayson Tatum and the preseason was an awesome start. Tatum averaged 21.0 points, 6.5 rebounds, 5.0 assists and 1.5 steals per game on 48% from the field and 39% from three in 28 minutes per game. His two-man game with Mitchell Robinson was one of the things that jumped off the page to me. pic.twitter.com/GpOUiNvvap — #LetsGoCeltics (@gobosceltics) October 17, 2026 — #LetsGoCeltics (@gobosceltics) October 17, 2026 pic.twitter.com/bumRblNDGU — #LetsGoCeltics (@gobosceltics) October 17, 2026 — #LetsGoCeltics (@gobosceltics) October 17, 2026 Tatum was also scoring in all his typical ways. He has gotten really good at splitting the defense on pick-and-rolls and getting to the rim for a layup or dunk. His three-point shot was very good, his defense was top notch, he was rebounding the ball, he was passing it well. He was doing all the things that he does when he is at his best. One note I do have is that J.T. does need to get to the line more; one free throw over two games isn’t nearly enough. He can very easily increase his scoring by just getting fouled more. 2. Offensive rebounding is going to be a massive advantage I wrote about this last week , but the Celtics are going to dominate the offensive boards. In their four preseason games, the Celtics had an offensive rebounding rate of 38.2%, which was the best in the preseason. Dominating the margins is something that Joe Mazzulla talks a lot about and one of those margins is the offensive glass as he wants to create extra possessions. Mitchell Robinson will play a big part in this. He is the best offensive rebounder in the NBA and on a team that is already really good at that, Robinson will fit right in. He was 2nd on the team for offensive rebounding in the preseason with Luka Garza leading Boston in that category. 3. Boston’s defense will force more turnovers I also wrote about this , but the Celtics are going go as far as their defense takes them. Boston is set up to have a defense on the level of the Thunder and Spurs. That is why I think this team has a high playoff ceiling. The preseason only confirmed these beliefs. In the two preseason games Boston played its starters, the Hornets had an offensive rating of 89.4 and the 76ers had an offensive rating of 95.5. It is the preseason and both Philly and Charolette were without some starters, but the Celtics defense has looked very good. One thing Boston has struggled with defensively in recent years is forcing turnovers. Last season, the Celtics ranked 23rd in opponent turnover percentage at 13.1%. In the two preseason games the starters played, the Sixers turnover percentage was 20.9% and the Hornets was 28.8% (they had 29 turnovers in the game). Paul George is going to be a big part of the Celtics forcing more turnovers. In the game against the Sixers, George had five steals. pic.twitter.com/ycfh0msxRP — #LetsGoCeltics (@gobosceltics) October 17, 2026 — #LetsGoCeltics (@gobosceltics) October 17, 2026 Forcing turnovers matters because it creates a fast break opportunity to get an easy shot on offense and it is a possession where a team doesn’t get a shot up. Brad Stevens and Joe Mazzulla know the Celtics need to create more turnovers and I expect them to do just that this season. 4. Payton Pritchard needs to start Enough is enough. It is time for Joe Mazzulla to insert Payton Pritchard to the starting lineup. I don’t know how much it really matters, but starting the game with your 2nd best offensive player on the bench is just not something I think the Celtics should be doing. Pritchard is plain and simply too good to not start. He had 25 points and 6 assists in his first preseason game and 19 points and 11 assists in his 2nd preseason game. Let’s not over think this — teams should start their best players in the NBA and Pritchard is one of the Celtics best players. He is ready to be the starting point guard so let him be the starting point guard. With that said, he probably won’t start and I will be annoyed on Twitter (I don’t like calling it X) every game he doesn’t. not starting payton is so unserious — jack (@janderson22_) October 14, 2026 (If they don’t start Payton, I’d rather start Baylor Scheierman than Jordan Walsh who started three preseason games.) 5. Hugo Gonzalez is really good and will probably be every national TV color guy’s favorite Celtic In the Celtics preseason finale on Friday in Philadelphia, Hugo Gonzalez had 21 points, 4 rebounds and 3 assists. Hugo Gonzalez 21 PTS, 6/10 FG, 6/8 FT vs 76ers https://t.co/iPMqMjOPeS — Every Bucket (@EveryBucketNBA) October 17, 2026 For the preseason, Gonzalez shot 63% from the field and 55% from three in the four games. He plays with such hustle, is a really good defender and is usually always in the right spot. Every national TV color analyst is going to talk about how much they love Hugo all season. In fact, Stan Van Gundy already said as much on the Zach Lowe Show this week. (You need to watch past the part of them talking about how to say Sandro Mamukelashvili’s name to get to the Hugo love.) Gonzalez is just really good. He makes a big impact on the game on both sides and is very quick in everything he does. His foot speed and decision making are chief among those. I think there may be a world where Hugo gets Sixth Man of the Year attention at the end of the season. 6. The Mitchell Robinson and Neemias Queta lineups are something I am interested in In the Hornets game, Mazzulla unleashed a new look that had Robinson and Queta share the floor for a few minutes. Unfortunately, I could not find what their plus minus or net rating was with them on the court but the eye test said it could work. Now, it won’t be a thing in the playoffs but in the regular season, I would like to see Joe try it out and see what it looks like. Both guys are good defenders and Robinson’s ability to move his feet and guard on the perimeter helps that a lot. The spacing could be clunky but there are ways to work around it. Give me a heavy dose of Mitch and Neem in real games. With Tatum that’s dunk city. Can’t play off either of them or you can flow into a pick and roll or DHO, OREBs for days, mobility on defense + 2rim protectors. — Trey (@TA1297) October 15, 2026 7. Neemias Queta threes might be a thing and I am not sure they should be I remember the days when Luke Kornet stopped shooting threes and everyone wanted him to let them fly again. There was no need for Luke Kornet to shoot threes on those teams and I don’t think there is a need for Neemias Queta to shoot threes on this team. Queta went 0/4 in the preseason; he did make the one with his toe on the line in the corner. His TOENAIL was on the line 😅 https://t.co/ZXHlFuNycU — Celtics on NBC Sports Boston (@NBCSCeltics) October 15, 2026 Let’s call him 1/5. If Neemy is going to be shooting 20% on threes, I don’t think he should be taking them. Now, it was pointed out several times in the broadcasts that Queta does take threes when he plays for Portugal in FIBA, but he was 0/2 in qualifiers this year and 2/7 in Euros last year. In a small sample size, it has not proven to be a good shot. As a result, I will remain a skeptic on Neemias Queta three-point shots. 8. Dillon Mitchell jumps off the screen My favorite moment of the preseason is when Dillon Mitchell sank a clutch pull up three in overtime of the Sixers game on Friday night. DILLON MITCHELL CLUTCH RIP AND RUN PULL UP 3 WE LIVE https://t.co/V0CGZTQ6OA — Nik Land | NikNBA🏀 (@NIKNBAYT) October 17, 2026 Mitchell was a bad three-point shooter in college and if he can find that in the league, the Celtics could have a useful player. Everything else he does jumps off the screen when you are watching him. He is a one of one athlete. How high he jumps and how fast he gets off the ground are two things that have stood out. He is also fast and has really long arms that make an impact on the defensive side of the court. The three-point shot is not promised to come but if it ever did, even if he just was consistently just above 30%, the Celtics could have a very good player on their hands. Also, Sam Cassell used him as a small ball 5 in overtime on Friday, which is something that raises my eyebrow. 9. Devin Carter was the right choice for the last two-way spot Carter only played in one of the four preseason games but he was still able to secure the last two-way spot, according to Michael Scotto. The Boston Celtics are converting Devin Carter to a two-way deal, league sources told @hoopshype. Carter averaged 8.9 points, 3.3 rebounds, and 2.7 assists in 18.4 minutes during 38 games for the Sacramento Kings last season. https://t.co/CZJQfZb4F6 — Michael Scotto (@MikeAScotto) October 17, 2026 Carter was a first round pick for the Sacramento Kings in 2024 and had an impressive debut for the Celtics in the win over the Cavaliers with 17 points, 5 rebounds, 3 assists and 2 steals. He flashed the potential that many thought he could show when he was the Big East Player of the Year for the Providence Friars in 2024. He was all over the court in the game against Cleveland and he will have a chance to make a real impact on the Celtics this year. He missed the last three preseason games due to an illness. 10. Preseason Champions! The Celtics went 4-0 in the preseason and that means they are the preseason champions (please note: I don’t know if anyone else went undefeated in the preseason). The last time the Celtics went undefeated in the preseason was 2019.

stories.title: YouTube Gold: The Willis Reed Game Remains Iconic
stories.summary: One of the most dramatic things ever seen in an NBA game.
stories.detailText: UNITED STATES - MAY 08: N.Y. Knicks Willis Reed [19] lets fly with shot against Wilt Chamberlain and the Los Anges Lakers in Game 7 of the 1969-70 NBA Finals. Knicks defeated the Lakers 113-99. (Photo by NY Daily News Archive via Getty Images) | NY Daily News via Getty Images T here have been some incredibly iconic moments in NBA history. Consider Julius Erving’s under-the-basket layup. Consider Michael Jordan pumping his fist after eliminating the Cleveland Cavaliers, or Jerry West hitting a 60-foot shot to put a Finals game vs. the Knicks into overtime…or Magic Johnson hitting that hook shot against the Boston Celtics in the Finals. Now consider Willis Reed in Game 7 of the 1970 Finals. Reed had torn his right quadricep, and that would be brutal for the average person walking around the house. In his case, he had to play professional basketball, and not only did he have to do that, his opposite number was Wilt Chamberlain, perhaps the most powerful athlete in American history. Up until game time, it wasn’t at all clear that Reed would be able to go. However, he got 200 ccs of Cortisol just before tip-off, and when he came out of the tunnel, the Knicks and their fans were electrified. Reed took the first two shots of the game, made both, and the game was effectively over. It was that powerful. It remains the definitive example of courage on a basketball court.
