teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Matt Kelley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders aim to avoid a three-game losing streak in Week 6 against the Buffalo Bills . To preview the game for Raider Nation, Silver and Black Pride reached out to our friends at Buffalo Rumblings, and Matt Byham was kind enough to answer a few questions about the Bills . Q: On paper, it doesn’t seem like Josh Allen has a go-to target this season since no pass-catcher enters Sunday with 20 receptions or 300 yards through five games. However, five players have double-digit catches and triple-digit receiving yards . So, is there a receiver or two who you think will make a big impact in Las Vegas? On a similar note, is there an alpha in the group that Allen will turn to if he needs a big play? A: At the start of the season, the Bills’ passing attack was humming along well with wide receiver DJ Moore and tight end Dalton Kincaid leading the charge. Moore finally brought back the WR1 skill set lacking since Stefon Diggs’ departure. Defenses were forced to account for him whenever and wherever he lined up. Moore’s addition really opened things up for Kincaid, who profiles like a huge and athletic wide receiver. Kincaid became the deep threat, and an efficient one at that. Moore suffered an AC joint sprain (separated shoulder) in Week 2, and that brought things crashing back down to Earth a bit. Moore has missed only one game (Los Angeles Rams, Week 5), playing through the pain rather than landing on in-season Injured Reserve. However, he’s understandably not been the same player since Week 1. Now teams can devote additional resources to take Kincaid away, and that’s all but eliminated the deep passing play. But all isn’t lost, with third-year wide receiver Keon Coleman taking a huge leap toward becoming a go-to target for Allen. Coleman isn’t a prototypical burner at receiver, but he’s someone who can play at any level of the passing attack. Through five games, Coleman has made 15 catches on 18 targets for 224 yards and two touchdowns. That’s a highly efficient stat line, which is made more impressive by his 11 catches for a first down. Coleman has proven to be reliable and an important part of the passing game this season. He also climbs an astonishingly high ladder, making contested catches look like routine grabs. I expect Coleman to play a featured role, regardless of Moore’s status. There’s also wide receiver Khalil Shakir, who may well fit the role of alpha. He often operates as Allen’s go-to in the early stages and in crunch time, and his chemistry with Allen acts as an irreplaceable rhythm setter. He’s a typical modern-day slot receiver, though Brady and Allen have tried to involve him downfield more. Shakir can take it to the house from the backfield if the defense doesn’t respect his speed and elusiveness in space. Then there’s running back Ty Johnson, the team’s third-down specialist. He’s an incredible receiver out of the backfield and the speediest player in the team’s running backs room. Johnson is a legit problem for defenses, and he’s likely to play a big role if Allen struggles to get things going with more traditional receiving options. Q: James Cook is a year removed from winning the NFL rushing title and is averaging 11 more rushing yards per game ( 95.4 to 106.4 ) so far in 2026. What makes him such a dynamic running back, and what’s led to the bump in efficiency this year, since he’s also averaging about a half-yard more per carry? (Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images) | Getty Images" data-portal-copyright="Getty Images" /> A: James Cook is incredibly talented, and it often looks like he’s on ice skates while everyone around him is stuck in mud. Cook’s agility and center of gravity are nearly unrivaled, able to take it to the house on one cut from any distance in a way that reminds me of Terrell Davis or even Marcus Allen. Regarding the efficiency bump, you can likely point to fresh legs at the start of the season and his lethal one-cut approach. He also has a strong group of offensive linemen who thoroughly enjoy slobber-knocking defenders to clear a path for Cook. To boot, Brady is doing a better job mixing plays up on first down in 2026, where in 2025 he’d often have Cook shoulder the load. Cook could be even better with added opportunity, despite a concerning amount of fumbles. He was discussed as the best dual-threat running back in his class, yet Cook is often an afterthought in the passing game. That and a perceived (and incorrect) notion that he’s a liability blocking on 3rd & Long means Cook comes off the field more than is ideal for a featured back. Briefly returning to the fumbles, it’s one of the biggest issues facing the offense right now. Early comments by Brady suggested that Cook needs to get it under control or risk losing snaps. He walked that back a bit and said that Cook’s too good to sideline for too long (and likely benefits from supportive encouragement rather than the doghouse approach McDermott employed). Defenders are tuned in to Cook’s fumble issue, and he faces a ton of punches on every carry. How he responds to that adversity this weekend could go a long way toward defining his season. Cook seems committed to improving, but it’s going to be an issue for him until he proves it’s fixed. Q: One matchup I’ll be keeping an eye on this Sunday is the Raiders’ edge rushers (Maxx Crosby and Malcolm Koonce) against the Bills’ offensive tackles (Dion Dawkins and Spencer Brown). What would you say Dawkins’ and Brown’s strengths and weaknesses are, especially in pass protection? A: I love this question and wish I were better-equipped to discuss the finer nuances of offensive line play. Dawkins is a force of nature. He’s bigger than life and one of the key engines to the Bills’ offense and a massive ambassador for the Buffalo area. He lost roughly 45 pounds in the offseason, which has allowed him to play with quicker feet and better twitch. Dawkins isn’t perfect and will occasionally surrender pressures to highly athletic, twitchy edge rushers. He’s best as a brick wall, whether backpedaling or bull rushing, but he can be beat if a defender forces him into sloppy technique. Spencer Brown looks like a professional wrestler who’s a better right tackle. A freak of nature in so many respects, Brown is a tsunami as a run blocker, and he’s athletic enough to take almost any defensive end to task headed his way en route to Allen. His height (6’8”) can be a detriment from time to time against edge rushers who like to anchor low pivots toward the pocket. Where Brown struggles most is with injuries. He’s dealt with a back issue in multiple seasons, with a flare-up forcing him out early against the Rams. Brown will play Sunday; it’s just a matter of how well his back holds up. Q: On the other side of the trenches, and in a similar vein, two Buffalo defensive linemen who have really caught fire this season are defensive end Greg Rousseau and defensive tackle Deone Walker. How would you describe their respective skill sets, and what has led to their ascension? (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images" data-portal-copyright="Getty Images" /> A: More massive human beings! Greg Rousseau (Bills Mafia calls him Groot) is a 6’7” nightmare for an offense. It’s fair to say that Rousseau was miscast in prior head coach Sean McDermott’s 4-3 system. Now playing outside linebacker for the first time in his career, Rousseau has more space to operate and cause havoc for linemen trying to engage with him. Rousseau is extremely fast for a defensive end, and his speed is magnified operating away from the trenches a bit. He’s playing a brand of football most had never seen before, combining a relentless motor with a physical profile seen only among the top 1% of his peers. Rousseau is a fun watch, and it’s possible he’s just getting started on a path to true greatness. Then there’s Deone Walker. Why did teams pass him up in the draft? Well, his size was part of the issue. At almost 6’8” and over 330 pounds, many wondered how and where Walker would fit in on the defensive line. Would he be able to hold anchor with a high center of gravity, and could he meet the athletic demands required of an NFL defensive lineman? Walker, an absolute unit, carved his own path, becoming a handful as a pass rusher no one could contain. Forget pegging him in as a run-stuffing defensive tackle. Walker is his own brand of special, and he refuses the confinement of pigeonholes. The best is yet to come with Walker, who also shed weight in the offseason. Now he looks the part of a 3-4 defensive lineman ready to be shot out of a cannon. If Walker’s on the field, he’s coming for the quarterback. In general, both players’ ascension ties back to the defensive change to an attacking mentality under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. The defense, and Leonhard, have come under a lot of fire early on — though they are sneaky good defending the run. That said, the defensive line (and by association the outside linebackers) is playing better football than anything seen in McDermott’s system (which was better against the pass). Leonhard’s system, which is essentially a hybrid of what he wants to ultimately run, has allowed Rousseau and Walker’s best attributes to shine. Once Leonhard gets more of the players he covets on defense, we could see another level unlocked for Rousseau and Walker. Q: That being said, the Bills’ defense comes into the game ranking 28th in points per game allowed (28.2) and 30th in yards allowed per game (404.0). If you were Klint Kubiak, how would you go about attacking Buffalo’s defense? A: I’d plan for a shootout and be well aware of how many consecutive wins the Bills have when giving up 31 points or more to opponents. It’s eight, including two such games this season. As such, I’m going down swinging for the fences because of Josh Allen. Interestingly, the Rams played keep-away with Allen Monday night. It worked to limit his opportunities in the first half, but they couldn’t keep Allen and the offense out of scoring range. That effort simply shortened the game, while failing to secure a lead at halftime. Keeping Allen on the sideline is a decent plan, but so far this season it only works well if the offense scores touchdowns on each possession. To that point, I wouldn’t waste a ton of time trying to establish a running game. Instead, I’d devote whatever resources are necessary to account for Rousseau and Walker, while testing the inside linebackers and defensive backs early and often. Kirk Cousins may not have a rocket for an arm, but he’s dangerous enough to find the flaws in Buffalo’s secondary. I fully expect Brock Bowers to take advantage of whoever tries to cover him. It might be smart to use Jeanty in the passing game to perhaps further open up plays downfield to other receivers. On defense, I’d constantly have a spy on Allen, and I’d fool him with pre-snap coverage “lies” that throw off his mojo post-snap. I’d have also probably spent a lot of time studying the film from Buffalo’s games against the Los Angeles Chargers and New England Patriots. If all else fails, then I’m spray-painting something on Allen’s jersey to tick off Maxx Crosby. This should be a fun game with a lot of offensive fireworks!

teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Joe Brady and Klint Kubiak represent a changing of the guard for the NFL. The Buffalo Bills’ and Las Vegas Raiders’ head coaches, respectively, are a pair of hotshot offensive play callers who ascended to the lead role of their franchises this past offseason. And through five games of the 2026 campaign, the neither team regrets the decision to go with offensive coordinators-turned-first-time lead men. The ascension of Brady, the 37-year-old who served as Buffalo’s offensive coordinator last season, appeared inevitable after the Bills dismissed then-head coach Sean McDermott in January following the team’s 33-30 overtime loss to the Denver Broncos in the AFC Division Round of the playoffs last season. Brady has picked up where he left off as he remains the play caller and head coach title as Buffalo (4-1 overall) is the top-ranked scoring offense (164 total points) and fourth-highest yards gained (1,981) in the NFL so far. The Bills red zone offense is the sixth-best with 15 touchdowns on 21 trips in the area between the opponent’s 20-yard line and end zone (a 71.4 percent success rate). Last season, Brady was the architect of Bills’ fourth-best scoring (481) and yards gained (6,397) offense. The red zone performance was impressive too in 2025 as Buffalo scored 43 touchdowns on 65 visits (66.2 percent success rate). #Bills HC Joe Brady, in the nicest and kindest way possible, put RB James Cook on notice over his fumbling issues. Brady said there will be consequences if it continues, including fewer carries. pic.twitter.com/LLv8bKI6k0 — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) October 13, 2026 Flipping to Kubiak, the 39-year-old has breathed much-needed life into an anemic Raiders offense that ranked dead last in points scored and yards gained in 2025 under a different regime. While many want to forget the abysmal 2025 campaign, the Silver & Black produced just 241 total points and 4,168 total yards which ranked 32nd out of the 32 teams in the league. Currently, Las Vegas (3-2) sits with the eighth-highest scoring offense (132) and 14th-most yards gained (1,678) through five games with Kubiak at the helm and with the play sheet, providing tangible data on why minority owner Tom Brady, general manager John Spytek, and the rest of the Raiders’ decision makers were deliberate and patient to interview and eventually hire Kubiak. There’s areas of opportunity for the Raiders head coach, however, such as a ground game that’s been neutralized and is in the bottom run of the league rankings (28th in yards gained at 402; 27th in rushing touchdowns at just two). Another blemish for Kubiak’s offense is red zone performance as the team has scored just 10 touchdowns on 18 visits (55.6 percent success rate) which ranks 20th in the NFL. That noted, Kubiak’s system has super veteran Kirk Cousins on-point as Raiders quarterback and is using elite tight end Brock Bowers all over the field. The synergy Kubiak has in Las Vegas is clearly lacking from his former team, the Seattle Seahawks (3-3). The Raiders head coach was Mike Macdonald’s offensive coordinator in Seattle and the Seahawks offense has struggled creating that rhythm Kubiak had as he orchestrated the third-best scoring offense (483) and eighth-best yards gained (5,973) for the 2025 Super Bowl champions. The Week 6 clash between the Bills and Raiders inside Allegiant Stadium features two young coaches in their respective AFC divisions (East for Buffalo, West for Las Vegas). And if both can continue their impressive debut seasons and beyond, are the changing of the guard from older and established coaches. Maxx Crosby speaks on the Raiders loss to the Patriots, what Klint Kubiak’s message was, & playing the Bills & Rams the next 2 weeks “The fans should be disappointed. We got whooped, but there are good things on film & things to get better at” pic.twitter.com/OXqBop5hNb — ShifftttyyyQB1✞🏴‍☠️ (@raiders1022) October 14, 2026 But first comes Sunday’s matchup where the Raiders are looking to rebound to keep pace in the AFC West while the Bills are eager to trample another opponent to remain in the AFC East lead. Kubiak heaped praise on Buffalo during his media sessions this week and he made it clear his offense must stay on the field and score points against the high-powered Bills. “Yeah, well, you’ve got to get first downs to stay on the field. So, going three and out and punting the ball back is not the way to go,” Kubiak said. “So, you’ve got to sustain drives. A big part of sustaining drives is not being one-dimensional. So, that’s a part of our team that we got to improve.” Keeping quarterback Josh Allen on the sideline as much as they can will help Las Vegas, especially as the Raiders defense has struggled mightily in the red zone (14 touchdowns allowed on 18 visits; 28th in the league). And Brady is well aware of the Silver & Black’s penchant to create turnovers — even though the Raiders have only one takeaway the last two weeks after forcing nine in the first three games of the season. Ball security is a must for Buffalo as running back James Cook and Allen have four fumbles, apiece. “Right now, we’re putting the ball in harm’s way, and we know that’s the way that we lose football games is we turn the ball over,” Brady said. “James has put the ball on the ground. He’s doing so many good things running the football, and I don’t want to lose sight of how great he is running the ball right now, but we’re putting the ball on the ground, and it’s negating all the positive. “And I have all the confidence in him. That’s why I put him right back out there. But obviously at some point there has to be consequences when we’re putting negative stuff out there. James knows. It’s important to him, but that can’t happen, and it’s going to cost us football games, and it almost cost us that one. So, it’s got to improve, or the carries are going to decrease.” Kubiak said Dont'e Thornton Jr. is "getting closer" to being activated from IR. On what he saw from him this week: "I'm impressed. He's looking good. He's getting back into football shape. Really doing a great job in the meeting room. He's putting himself in position." https://t.co/GcZhA4y0EO — Sam Warren (@samwarren83) October 16, 2026 While both Kubiak and Brady are younger head coaches, the inherent roster differences between the Raiders and Bills is quite the advantage for the Bills. There’s just simply more talent on Brady’s roster than Kubiak’s due, in large part, to Buffalo’s sustained success of seven-straight winning seasons from 2019-25. Las Vegas has only one season in Sin City where they were above .500 — a 10-7 record in 2021, in comparison. That said, stranger things have happened and it’s not out of the realm of possibility for Las Vegas to get a much-needed victory at home. Quotes of Note “Yeah, that’s the best tool. You know, the guys are visual. You can only tell them so much. If you show them, it definitely helps get your point across. That’s definitely something that I like to do, a lot of coaches on our staff like to do. But you got to make the correction somehow, someway. So, whatever hits the player’s brain the fastest you got to use that technique.” —Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak on how game film from last Sunday’s loss helps his team. “Benefits? I don’t know if there are benefits from getting your butt whooped, but you got to know yourself in your area, your strengths and your weaknesses on defense.” —Las Vegas Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard when asked if last Sunday’s game tape benefits the team.

teamStories.title: Raiders Mailbag: Is Spencer Burford offensive line’s biggest problem?
teamStories.summary: It’s funny how two weeks can dramatically change the tune of an entire season. The Las Vegas Raiders have gone from a feel-good story as one of the biggest surprises in the NFL to feeling like the sky is falling. Back-to-back losses, including an embarrassing blowout in New England last week, will do that. Part […]
teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s funny how two weeks can dramatically change the tune of an entire season. The Las Vegas Raiders have gone from a feel-good story as one of the biggest surprises in the NFL to feeling like the sky is falling. Back-to-back losses, including an embarrassing blowout in New England last week, will do that. Part of the reason is the Raiders’ offensive line continues to be an issue, as it’s a major point of emphasis in this week’s mailbag (again) heading into Week 6 against the Buffalo Bills . Q: I’ve seen a couple of other guys on Raider Twitter saying that Spencer Burford has been the best guard still, and his PFF grades are more affected because they mostly help the other side. Sorta similar to DJ Glaze. I think Marcus, in one of the TDLs, said he was the best run blocker for that game. He seems to get beat a lot in pass pro every game, though. What do you think about that? Do you feel run or pass pro is more important and that affects the choice? It kinda seems like the guards have all been bad, but at some point the decision is if they are gonna be bad anyway, then you might as well work on the upside of Caleb Rogers or Trey Zuhn III. Also, if the Raiders are gonna throw Fernando Mendoza in there, they’ve gotta protect him better, right? A: When it comes to pass protection versus run blocking at guard, I tend to lean toward the running game . Of course, both are requirements of the position. However, in my opinion, pass protection is easiest at guard — compared to the other two offensive line positions — since they (typically) aren’t responsible for setting the protection and doing the thinking for a group like a center is. Also, guards have help on both sides with a center and a tackle to their left and right, and interior pass-rushers don’t have as much space to operate, unlike blocking on the edge. So while it’s ideal to have a guard who can do both at a high level, personally, I’ll sacrifice some pass-pro issues for a high-level run blocker. Burford is decent in the running game and has had a couple of good outings in that department. For some context, Pro Football Focus gave him a 73.9 run-blocking grade against the Saints and an 81.0 against the Chiefs. One of those two is the game Marcus referenced. However, Burford has a 56.6 mark for the season. To be clear, I’m not trying to say PFF grades are the end-all, be-all; I’m just using them to contextualize the level of “good” versus “bad” and Burford’s performance. The problem is, and this is true pretty much regardless of what website or metric you’re using, he’s given up the most pressures ( 18 ) of any guard in the league and has the fourth-lowest pass protection grade (26.6). To me, just being decent or slightly above-average as a run blocker isn’t worth the liability he’s been when protecting the quarterback, even given my preference for the position. Also, as you mentioned, Mendoza is going to take over at some point. Having a young quarterback shifts the goalposts because putting the future of the franchise behind bad pass protection is organizational malpractice. That’s where even I would say it makes more sense to give a guy like Zuhn, who doesn’t bring much as a run blocker but was good in pass protection at tackle in college, so the rookie signal-caller doesn’t get killed. I think the narrative that Burford was getting less help was true during the first three weeks of the season. However, in the last two games, he’s been getting a lot more help from Kolton Miller in pass protection. When the Raiders want to push the ball down the field, Miller has been staying closer to the line of scrimmage a little longer so that he can help slow the defensive tackle down. More on this in the next question; that’s also part of the left tackle’s issues. At the end of the day, both guards have left something to be desired. Jackson Powers-Johnson continues to be inconsistent, especially as a run blocker, but he’s at least been solid in pass protection. So, he and Burford both could get replaced, and it wouldn’t surprise me if Klint Kubiak does that soon. But, in my opinion, Kubiak at least has to give someone else a shot at left guard. The thing to keep in mind about Burford is that the only reason he started games during his last two years in San Francisco was because of injuries. On top of that, Ben Bartch was the 49ers’ starting left guard in Weeks 1 and 2 before getting injured, and they turned to Connor Colby before Burford after Bartch went down last season. I get the “scheme fit” and “familiarity with the system” line of thinking, but Burford didn’t have the track record to be unchallenged for the starting spot in training camp. If you ask me, it’s time for Kubiak to try someone else at that spot. Q: What is going on with Kolton Miller? Is he injured, or is FatherTime finally catching up with him? A: I got this question last week and defended Miller, saying he only had one bad game at the time. Then, he went out and had another bad game. (Thanks for having my back, Kolton, LOL!). So, I definitely think left tackle is something to monitor for the rest of the year, especially as we creep closer to the offseason and start thinking about team needs. The 31-year-old likely doesn’t have that many years left, after all, and he certainly needs to play better. However, picking up where I left off above, I don’t think it’s a coincidence that Miller’s struggles began the week after Burford gave up a season-high six pressures and posted a 4.0 PFF pass-blocking grade against the Saints. As previously mentioned, the left tackle has been giving the guard more help in pass protection, and the clip Marcus posted below is a good example. This was a bad sack by Cousins. He had Tucker open, and I'm not sure why he came off it. Then just stares down Bowers. Knocked the Raiders out of field goal range. pic.twitter.com/qt56gT2KwL — Marcus Johnson (@TheMarcJohnNFL) October 12, 2026 The endzone view (which starts around the 20-second mark) gives you a good look at what I’m talking about when I say Miller has to stay closer to the line of scrimmage at first. Notice how he doesn’t get much depth on his pass set initially and extends his inside arm. That’s to give the defensive tackle (No. 97) less space to operate and potentially get another hand on the DT to help slow his momentum down for Burford. Compare Miller’s pass set to DJ Glaze’s on the other side. Since the center is turning to the right and able to help JPJ, Glaze doesn’t have to worry about assisting the guard and can get depth immediately. Whereas Miller has to hang tight for a second and then rush to get depth, throwing his footwork and the whole process out of whack because the process has to be sped up. On top of that, Burford loses on the high side of the rush, forcing Kirk Cousins to step up in the pocket. As a result, the edge rusher works back inside and Miller, who can’t see where the quarterback is, gives up a sack. Don’t get me wrong, Miller has to do a better job of staying engaged on the block and staying in front of inside moves is part of playing tackle. But the point I’m making here is that his assignment is more difficult because the guy next to him isn’t getting the job done. So, both guards are getting help in this example. However, one of them was brought in to be a reliable veteran who knows the system, and the other had to fight to retain his starting spot during training camp. Again, a case could be made for both guys to get replaced, but I don’t know how anyone can justify Burford’s level of play this season. And when it comes to Miller, he definitely needs to pick it up, too. But I’d like to see how he plays with someone else next to him. Q: I like outside zone running, but maybe the line, which we thought was suited for it, really isn’t. Why not move JPJ to left guard, where he had played better in the past, and try Evan Neal at right guard and run more power/gap? We need some beef on the O-line! A: The Raiders’ rushing attack has been pretty balanced this season, with 60 zone runs to 57 gap runs, according to Sumer Sports . Also, every starting offensive lineman has a better PFF run-blocking grade in zone than gap. Based on that data, the latter is the bigger problem. But to your point about moving Powers-Johnson to the left side, I think that should be on the table, too. He played well there as a rookie, and Caleb Rogers can slide in at right guard since that’s where Rogers has been getting reps. I have my doubts that Neal is the answer, but I’ll take just about anyone other than Burford at this point. At the end of the day, a change just has to be made because the Raiders can’t continue to have such a lackluster rushing attack. Q: Are the OL issues because of mismatched players/scheme fits, that haven’t played together long enough, or coaching that isn’t resonating with the players? At times they look lost out there. A: I’ve touched on most of this already, but the chemistry piece is a factor, too. The interior three have never worked together before this season, and while JPJ and Glaze were in the same draft class, they’ve hardly been next to each other. Powers-Johnson played left guard and center as a rookie, and then missed over half of last season. So, there is some validity to the argument that the line needs more time to gel together, especially since zone runs require more cohesion up front. But the clock is also ticking… Q: Can JJ Pegues improve the Raiders’ pass rush? Should they be looking at practice squad DTs and free agents? Their practice squad DTs have potential as NTs but offer limited pass rush upside. I guess it really depends on how low the bar has been set by Jonah Laulu, Thomas Booker IV and Adam Butler. A: For some context here, I posted on X/Twitter earlier this week that Booker has the highest pass-rush win rate of any Raiders defensive tackle so far this season at 8.5%, according to PFF. The problem is he’s recorded the second-fewest pass-rush snaps (63) of the team’s defensive tackles who have played in at least four games, and that rate ranks 48th among defensive tackles league-wide. In other words, the defense is getting almost no pressure from its interior pass-rushers, and Booker isn’t winning frequently enough to simply just play him more. The bigger problem is that Pegues, or any of the other reserve defensive tackles, aren’t going to solve this problem. He’s more of a run defender, as are Brandon Cleveland and Tim Keenan III, as you mentioned. The interior pass-rusher who needs to step up the most is Tonka Hemingway. He has the skill set and has shown a few flashes but isn’t consistent enough right now. Maybe John Spytek and Co. can find a diamond in the rough from another team’s practice squad or a street free agent, but the odds are pretty low. Ultimately, I think this is something that will leak into the offseason, and Spytek needs to do a much better job of prioritizing the position than he has in the past. Q: Maxx doesn’t seem to be having a heavy impact on games even with his “pressures.” Per PFN, Maxx Crosby is tied for 58th in the NFL with a 6.7% pressure-to-sack ratio. Whether or not the Raiders are contending for a playoff spot as we move towards November, if a team offers a 1st, Spy would be crazy not to take it. Would you agree? (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images" data-portal-copyright="Getty Images" /> A: I know some people are getting frustrated with Crosby getting pressures but only having two sacks this season, and I think that comes down to a misunderstanding of what the stats show. Sacks happen when pressure is paired with good coverage. It’s no coincidence that the Broncos led the NFL in sacks during each of the last two seasons while having a two-time All-Pro corner in Patrick Surtain II. So, numbers like pressures and pass-rush win rate are used to isolate how the player is performing outside of the supporting cast. In other words, those figures help answer the question of: “Is Maxx Crosby (or whatever pass-rusher) doing his job?” PFF has Crosby tied for fourth among edge rushers with 30 pressures and fourth outright in win rate (20.9%), while having the second-highest double team rate . He is doing his job while opposing offenses are making it more difficult via chip blocks and sliding the protection to him. That’s on top of the coverage being shaky over the last two weeks, allowing the quarterbacks to find quick answers in the passing game. Also, sacks from edge rushers can come when the defensive tackles force the quarterback to step up in or bail out of the pocket. The clip above that I broke down with Burford and Miller is a good example of that. As I mentioned in my previous answer, that’s not happening in Vegas, either. I get it, a sack is the best stat a pass-rusher can have, and people want to see Crosby at the top of the charts. But there’s a lot more that goes into it than just his performance. As far as a trade goes, it’d still have to be more than just a first-round pick for me to get on board with that. Q: Why do you think Mike Washington Jr. is not getting more reps when it was reported that Kubiak wanted to draft him? A: I think a big part of it is the passing game. Washington wasn’t a good receiver or pass protector at Arkansas, and that has carried over into the NFL. Hence why Dylan Laube got more playing time last week. Also, Washington had a bad game against the Chiefs (Marcus mentioned on TDL that he had a missed or bad read that would have resulted in a touchdown), and I think Kubiak might have overreacted to that in New England. Additionally, being down 28-7 after the first position in the third quarter means the offense doesn’t have enough time left to run the ball much in the second half. The rookie running back’s workload will be something to keep tabs on this Sunday to see if Kubiak makes an adjustment Q: While I know the wide receivers have been a disappointment for not separating in their routes, doesn’t some of the blame go on Kubiak for not being able to “scheme” them open? He seems to be able to scheme Bowers open, and he doesn’t need his help. Other great offensive minds seem able to scheme their guys open all the time. Kubiak has done it a couple of times this year but not very often. A: Kubiak definitely seems to focus on scheming his top offensive weapon open rather than the supporting cast. For example, Jaxon Smith-Njigba was the Seahawks’ leading receiver last year with 119 catches and 1,793 yards, while no other pass-catcher even reached 55 catches and 600 yards during the regular season. So, that seems like one of the play-caller’s shortcomings. But I will say that there have been a decent number of plays where a wide receiver (primarily Tre Tucker) has gotten open, and Kirk Cousins either didn’t have enough time or was staring down Bowers too long. Cousins also has a reputation for checking the ball down quickly, and that’s another factor that can make the wideouts look worse. Now, I will 100% acknowledge that the Raiders have a talent problem at wide receiver, which will likely be another offseason need. But there are external factors like Kubiak and Cousins that have contributed to the lack of production from the position group. We know the current quarterback is a temporary situation, so the bigger factor moving forward is the play caller making some adjustments. Q: Kwity Paye began the season with a great game against Miami (6 tackles and 2 sacks), but it’s been downhill ever since. He had pedestrian performances against the Chargers (2 tackles) and the Saints (3 tackles). His last two games have been abysmal performances against the Chiefs (0 tackles) and the Patriots (1 tackle). I’m interested in your take on Kwity’s weaknesses and what he needs to do to be the impact player that Spytek and Rob Leonard thought he’d be? A: At the end of the day, Paye is a complementary piece rather than a playmaker. He has enough skill and a good motor to clean things up on the defensive line — that’s primarily what he did in the season opener — but isn’t someone who will be consistently productive without contributions from the defense’s main characters. The problem is that type of player isn’t worth $16 million a year. For comparison, Paye is making one million less than Chase Young and Alex Highsmith . Young is the primary pass-rusher in New Orleans and can be productive on his own. Highsmith plays second fiddle to T.J. Watt in Pittsburgh, but he can also win one-on-one matchups and be productive, fitting the second edge-rusher mold perfectly. Now, I mentioned last week that I’ll give Paye some grace since we aren’t even at the halfway point of the season yet. But as the weeks go by and he continues to be underwhelming, that signing continues to get closer and closer to being a bust. Q: Am I wrong for believing John Spytek is part of the problem? His 2025 draft class is looking like a complete bust, and 2026’s draft is looking shaky now. He’s failed to improve the WR room, and his free-agent signings have been suspect at best. A: Someone else asked: What are Spytek’s best and worst moves in the draft and free agency, and what grade would I give him so far? I think a C is a fair assessment for Spytek. Pete Carroll had way too much influence and control over last year’s roster, so I don’t think it’s fair to judge the general manager off the 2025 campaign. On top of that, building a quality roster that is sustainable for the long haul takes several years and draft classes to build, and we haven’t even seen two full seasons during his tenure in Las Vegas. That being said, Spytek has made plenty of Day 2 picks who aren’t seeing the field right now, and free-agent signings like Paye and Jalen Nailor have underwhelming production so far. With that in mind, I’m not going to pound the table and say Spytek has done anything more than an average job, landing on a ‘C’ grade. I know people aren’t going to want to hear this, but I also think Raider Nation needs to be more patient with Spytek. To me, it seems like he wanted to tear the roster down and start the rebuild last year, only to have that plan get blocked by Carroll, forcing him to delay the process by a year. He wasn’t going to fix all the problems and patch all of the holes in one offseason. Remember, expectations were pretty low heading into the season given the lack of talent on the roster. The 3-0 start changed things, but this is still a team that is in year one of a two-year rebuild. As far as best and worst moves: Nakobe Dean has been Spytek’s best free agent signing, and worst was Alex Cappa. Draft picks: I’ll go with Darien Porter for best (Treydan Stukes is a close second), and Charles Grant for worst. Granted, the sample size is the smallest, but I think Porter has been the best corner on the roster this season, and Grant isn’t seeing the field. I’m still a believer in the William & Mary product, but only having 59 snaps from a Top 100 pick is a bad investment so far. Q: There have been even more calls to bench Kirk Cousins since last week, and the team looked dismal versus the Pats as they fell to 3-2. What say you now? A: I still think the move is to roll with Cousins for now. However, if the Raiders lose this week, which I think they will, then the conversation really heats up. The problem is that the Rams are the next team up, and throwing Mendoza behind an offensive line that has been shaky recently against that pass rush probably isn’t a good idea. Plus, at 3-3, the coaching staff can convince themselves that the team is still in playoff contention. So, I think the sweet spot is going to be Week 8 against the Jets, especially if the Raiders drop the next two games. At 3-4 with four straight losses, that would mean Cousins isn’t keeping the playoff hopes alive, so Kubiak would have even more reason to make the change. That would, at least temporarily, help reignite the team’s postseason chances while simultaneously giving the No. 1 about half a season’s worth of starts to build on and grow from moving forward. That’ll do it for this week’s mailbag. Thank you all for submitting questions and, as your weekly reminder, if you’d like to have your questions answered in a future column, tweet them at me, @MHolder95 , email them to SBPQuestions1@gmail.com or look for our weekly call for questions on the site. The latter will continue to publish on Thursdays.
